flags.note: The construction 'שֶׁלֹּא יֵשׁ לָהֶם' (who not there is to them) is awkward. Native Hebrew would use 'אֲשֶׁר אֵין לָהֶם' or a simple relative clause.
The temporal clause 'בְּאִם שֶׁנּוֹשֵׁךְ' (when one bites) uses שֶׁ + participle, which may reflect Greek temporal clause structure rather than typical Hebrew temporal expressions.
While 'שֶׁל' constructions exist in later Hebrew, the frequent use throughout this text may indicate Greek influence on genitive expression.
The relative clause 'שֶׁתָּקַע' (who sounded) could be expressed more naturally in Biblical Hebrew as 'אֲשֶׁר תָּקַע'.
The construction 'מַלְבּוּשִׁים שֶׁל זֶפֶת' (garments of pitch) uses שֶׁל where native Hebrew would likely use construct state or simple genitive.
The relative clause 'שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם' (who had to them) is awkward; native Hebrew would use a simpler construction or different word order.
The relative clause 'שֶׁלֹּא יוּמְתוּ' (who were not killed) uses שֶׁ where 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא' might be more natural in Biblical Hebrew.
Another שֶׁ relative clause where 'אֲשֶׁר' might be expected in more classical Hebrew.
The construction 'שֶׁלֹּא יֵשׁ בָּהֶם' (which not there is in them) is awkward; native Hebrew would prefer 'אֲשֶׁר אֵין בָּהֶם'.
The construction 'וְשֶׁלֹּא עָשׂוּ' (and those who not did) continues the pattern of שֶׁ relatives that may reflect Greek influence.
